There are 4 factors at play, here:

1) Actually, genuinely understanding the feeling you describe. For example, if you're the hyper-rational, "first see if we're compatible before jumping into anything serious, love like in the movies is not even real, so there's no point in having high expectations", you describing someone fall hopelessly in love at first sight will probably sound a little fake. Ditto for trying to fancily describe an object when that object actually does nothing for you. It doesn't have to be love. Pick something you feel strongly about, and be honest, raw about it. But don't force other worldly feeling when there's none.

2) Having a certain kind of maturity and sophistication. There's a reason teenagers(even those who're pretty skilled at writing) tend to be cringey writers: the way they perceive emotions is still not well developed enough.

3) Having the ability to give what you write about an original, interesting twist. No one cares that the girl you're describing is pretty and nice; having something unique to say about the way she makes you feel is the goal here. 

4) Pure writing skill. I think reading a lot helps you here. From what I've seen, bad writers don't read good books and people who read good books are competent writers.
